title: Records, Enums and Streams
summary: Model data with records and enums, match sealed types with switch patterns, write lambdas and method references, and process collections with the Stream API.
introduction: Modern Java is noticeably shorter than the Java of ten years ago. Records declare an immutable data class in one line, enums give a fixed set of named values real behaviour, sealed interfaces and switch patterns let the compiler check that every case is handled, and the Stream API turns loops full of temporary lists into readable pipelines of filter, map and collect. This lesson introduces each feature with a complete program, shows the exact output, and points out the one stream mistake everybody makes once.
learningObjectives: Declare records with validation and extra methods
Define enums with fields and switch over them exhaustively
Combine sealed interfaces, records and switch pattern matching
Build stream pipelines with lambdas, method references and collectors

blocks.text: A **record** (Java 16) is a class whose whole purpose is to carry data. You list the components once and the compiler generates the constructor, an accessor per component (`name()`, not `getName()`), `equals`, `hashCode` and a readable `toString`. Components are `final`, so records are immutable. A **compact constructor** with no parameter list runs before the fields are assigned and is the place for validation, and you may add ordinary methods.

blocks.title: Shop.java
java Shop.java
blocks.content:
Pen costs 2.5
Product[name=Pen, price=2.5, category=office]
true
3.0
price must not be negative

blocks.text: Two records with the same component values are `equals`, which a hand-written class only achieves after overriding `equals` and `hashCode` correctly. Use a record whenever a class is a plain bundle of values: a point, a money amount, a row from a query, a message. Use a class when the object has identity or changes over time, such as the `BankAccount` from [Classes and Objects](/tutorials/java/classes-objects).

An **enum** is a type with a fixed set of named instances. Compared with string constants it cannot be misspelled, is checked by the compiler, and can carry fields, constructors and methods. `values()` lists the constants in declaration order, `valueOf` parses a name, `ordinal()` gives the position and `name()` the text. A `switch` over an enum that lists every constant needs no `default`; add a constant later and the compiler flags every switch expression that forgot it.

blocks.title: Cups.java
java Cups.java
blocks.content:
MEDIUM holds 350 ml
1 MEDIUM
SML
true

blocks.text: A `sealed` interface (Java 17) names exactly which types may implement it with `permits`. Together with records it models a closed set of alternatives, and since Java 21 a `switch` can match on the **type** of the value and even **deconstruct** a record into its components in the case label. Because the set is closed, the compiler verifies that every permitted type is covered and no `default` is needed. A `when` clause adds a condition to a case; cases are tested top to bottom, so the guarded case goes first.

blocks.title: Areas.java

blocks.text: A **lambda** is a short anonymous function: parameters, an arrow and a body. It can be passed wherever a **functional interface** (an interface with one abstract method) is expected: `Function` maps a value to another, `Predicate` tests a value, `Comparator` orders two. A **method reference** such as `Product::name` is a lambda that only calls one existing method. Streams are built from these.

blocks.title: Inside main (with java.util.function imports)

blocks.text: A **stream** is a pipeline over a source such as a list: **intermediate** operations (`filter`, `map`, `sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`) describe transformations and return a new stream, and one **terminal** operation (`toList`, `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `max`, `forEach`) runs the whole pipeline and produces a result. Nothing happens until the terminal operation. Read a pipeline top to bottom as a sentence: from the products, keep the cheap ones, order them by price descending, take their names, collect into a list.

blocks.title: Report.java
java Report.java
blocks.content:
[Mug, Notebook, Pen]
49.5
{kitchen=2, office=2}
Pen, Notebook, Mug, Kettle
55
Kettle

items: `toList()` (Java 16) returns an unmodifiable list; `collect(Collectors.toList())` is the older spelling.
`mapToDouble` and `IntStream` work on primitives and offer `sum`, `average`, `min` and `max` directly.
`Collectors.groupingBy` builds a map from a key function; the `TreeMap::new` argument keeps the keys sorted so the output is predictable.
`max` returns an `Optional`, a box that is empty when the stream had no elements; `orElse` supplies the fallback instead of risking `null`.

blocks.title: A stream can be used once
blocks.text: Storing a stream in a variable and running two terminal operations on it, for example `count()` and then `toList()`, throws `IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed`. Create a new stream from the collection for each pipeline; `products.stream()` is cheap. Also keep lambdas inside a pipeline free of side effects such as adding to an outside list; let the terminal operation produce the result.

blocks.title: Loops or streams?
blocks.text: Streams shine when a transformation reads naturally as filter, map, collect. For a loop that updates several variables, breaks early or does input and output, a plain `for` is clearer. Readability decides, and both compile to the same kind of bytecode.

questions.question: A record automatically provides a constructor, accessor methods, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`.
questions.explanation: That is the point of records: declare the components once and the compiler generates the boilerplate, with immutable fields.

questions.question: Which stream operation is terminal, meaning it actually runs the pipeline?
questions.explanation: `filter`, `map` and `sorted` are intermediate and lazy; they only describe the pipeline. `toList` is terminal and triggers the work.
